```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gtsummary)
library(gt)
library(broom)
library(knitr)
library(scales)

navy <- "#17365D"
teal <- "#18A999"

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        color = navy
      ),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
)

# Wellness Ranch GA4 export
data_file <- "wellness_ranch_ga4.csv"

# This analysis expects a session-level metric export,
# aggregated by device category and acquisition channel.
# Required fields:
# deviceCategory
# sessionDefaultChannelGroup
# sessions
# engagedSessions
# averageSessionDuration

required_columns <- c(
  "devicecategory",
  "sessiondefaultchannelgroup",
  "sessions",
  "engagedsessions",
  "averagesessionduration"
)

data_available <- file.exists(data_file)
analysis_ready <- FALSE
regression_ready <- FALSE

if (data_available) {

  ga4 <- read.csv(
    data_file,
    check.names = FALSE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  # Standardize exported GA4 field names
  names(ga4) <- gsub(
    "[^a-z0-9]",
    "",
    tolower(names(ga4))
  )

  analysis_ready <- all(
    required_columns %in% names(ga4)
  )

  if (analysis_ready) {

    ga4 <- ga4 |>
      transmute(
        device = as.factor(devicecategory),
        channel = as.factor(
          sessiondefaultchannelgroup
        ),
        sessions = as.numeric(sessions),
        engaged = as.numeric(engagedsessions),
        duration = as.numeric(
          averagesessionduration
        )
      ) |>
      filter(
        !is.na(device),
        !is.na(channel),
        !is.na(sessions),
        !is.na(engaged),
        !is.na(duration),
        sessions > 0,
        engaged >= 0,
        engaged <= sessions,
        duration >= 0
      )

    ga4 <- ga4 |>
      mutate(
        not_engaged = sessions - engaged,
        engagement_rate = engaged / sessions
      )

    analysis_ready <- nrow(ga4) > 0

    if (analysis_ready) {

      regression_ready <-
        nrow(ga4) >= 20 &&
        n_distinct(ga4$device) >= 2 &&
        n_distinct(ga4$channel) >= 2 &&
        n_distinct(ga4$duration) >= 2
    }
  }
}
```

# Prompt 1: Capabilities of gtsummary

## Essay Prompt 1

> In Step 1, you have seen how to create a summary table and modify it for various statistical analyses. Summarize the package's capabilities as explained by the speaker. How may the {gtsummary} benefit you for your school work or career?

---

## Understanding gtsummary

The gtsummary package provides a convenient way to generate formatted statistical tables directly from R.

Its main advantage is that it combines statistical reporting and presentation formatting in a consistent workflow.

Instead of manually copying results into tables, researchers can generate tables directly from their analysis code.

Important capabilities include:

::: {.incremental}
- Descriptive statistics using frequencies, percentages, means, medians, and standard deviations.
- Comparisons between groups.
- Hypothesis-testing results and p-values.
- Cross-tabulation of categorical variables.
- Regression model reporting.
- Customization of table labels, headers, and numerical formatting.
:::

The package allows statistical tables to be reproduced when the underlying dataset changes.

---

## Important gtsummary Functions

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `tbl_summary()` | Creates descriptive summary tables |
| `tbl_cross()` | Summarizes relationships between categorical variables |
| `add_p()` | Adds statistical significance tests |
| `add_overall()` | Includes overall summary statistics |
| `add_n()` | Displays sample sizes |
| `tbl_regression()` | Formats regression model results |
| `modify_header()` | Customizes table headings |
| `as_gt()` | Converts output into a gt table |

These functions make it easier to create consistent statistical reports without extensive manual formatting.

---

## Example: Professional Summary Table

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gtsummary-example
#| tbl-cap: "Example of a Statistical Summary Table"

trial |>
  select(
    age,
    grade,
    response,
    trt
  ) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = trt,
    missing = "no"
  ) |>
  add_overall() |>
  add_p() |>
  bold_labels()
```

This example uses the built-in gtsummary trial dataset to demonstrate how descriptive statistics and hypothesis tests can be combined into one table.

---

## How gtsummary Benefits My Schoolwork

For academic assignments, gtsummary can improve both efficiency and presentation quality.

The package is useful because it:

- Reduces repetitive formatting tasks.
- Organizes statistical results consistently.
- Makes research findings easier to compare.
- Supports reproducible statistical reporting.
- Integrates with Quarto for HTML reports and presentations.

I see particular value in using gtsummary for research assignments that require multiple tables and statistical tests.

Rather than spending time manually formatting results, I can focus more attention on selecting appropriate methods and interpreting the findings.

---

For example, our team could use statistical tables to compare website engagement across acquisition channels and device categories.

We could also summarize website performance indicators and analyze relationships among traffic and engagement measures.

These analyses could help identify areas where digital marketing strategies may need further evaluation.

**My main takeaway is that gtsummary helps bridge the gap between technical statistical output and professional business reporting.**

# Prompt 2: Extended gtsummary Presentation

## Essay Prompt 2

> In Step 2, you watched the extended presentation of the {gtsummary} package by Dr. Daniel Sjoberg, the creator of the package.
>
> 2.1. How does it differ from gt and gtExtras?
>
> 2.2. Give three things you learned newly that were not explained in the lecture in Step 1.

---

## Prompt 2.1: gtsummary vs. gt vs. gtExtras

Although these three packages can be used together, each focuses on a different aspect of reporting.

| Package | Main Purpose |
|---|---|
| gtsummary | Creating statistical summary and regression tables |
| gt | Creating and styling general-purpose tables |
| gtExtras | Providing additional visual and formatting features for gt tables |

The most important distinction is that gtsummary is designed specifically for statistical reporting.

The gt package provides a more general system for presenting data in tables, while gtExtras extends the visual capabilities of gt.

---

## How the Three Packages Work Together

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Statistical Analysis

**gtsummary**

- Descriptive statistics
- Group comparisons
- Hypothesis testing
- Regression summaries
- Statistical formatting

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

### Visual Presentation

**gt and gtExtras**

- Table titles and subtitles
- Fonts, colors, and layout
- Conditional formatting
- Embedded visual indicators
- Additional styling options

:::

:::

A useful approach is to create the statistical table using gtsummary and then use gt to further customize its appearance.

This separates the statistical analysis from the visual design while maintaining a reproducible workflow.

---

## Example: Combining gtsummary and gt

```{r}
#| label: tbl-styled-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Customized Statistical Table"

trial |>
  select(
    age,
    grade,
    trt
  ) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = trt,
    missing = "no"
  ) |>
  add_p() |>
  bold_labels() |>
  as_gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Statistical Summary",
    subtitle = "Comparison of Treatment Groups"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_options(
    table.font.size = gt::px(14)
  )
```

This example demonstrates how statistical reporting and table styling can be integrated into one workflow.

---

## Prompt 2.2: Three Advanced Capabilities

Three additional capabilities that extend beyond basic summary-table creation are particularly valuable to my learning.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

**1. Regression models can be automatically formatted.**

The `tbl_regression()` function can convert fitted statistical models into readable tables with coefficients, confidence intervals, and p-values.

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

**2. Table formatting can be extensively customized.**

Functions such as `modify_header()` and `modify_footnote_header()` allow analysts to adjust how statistical information is presented.

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

**3. Multiple statistical tables can be combined.**

Functions including `tbl_merge()` and `tbl_stack()` allow several analyses to be brought together into a coordinated report.

:::

::: aside
These are advanced capabilities documented by gtsummary. Their exact coverage in the assigned Step 2 video should be confirmed against the lecture.
:::

---

## Why These Capabilities Matter

These features are important because real-world analysis often involves more than one statistical test or table.

For example, the Wellness Ranch CEP project could require descriptive summaries, comparisons between website visitor groups, and regression analysis.

Using compatible reporting functions would help maintain a consistent format across these analyses.

I also learned that combining packages is often more effective than relying on one package to perform every task.

This approach can make an analytical workflow more flexible and easier to maintain.

---

## Reflection on Prompt 2

My understanding of gtsummary has expanded from basic summary-table generation to a broader statistical reporting workflow.

The package is useful not only because it produces attractive tables, but also because it reduces the need to manually extract and organize model results.

The relationship among gtsummary, gt, and gtExtras also demonstrates the importance of choosing tools based on their strengths.

For future projects, including Wellness Ranch, I would use gtsummary for statistical content and gt or gtExtras when additional presentation customization is needed.

# Prompt 3: Cross-Tabulation Analysis

## Essay Prompt 3

> Apply what you learned to your MSDM CEP data. Choose two appropriate variables for cross-tabulation and show if the two variables are associated or not. Use appropriate statistics to test if the two variables are associated. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.

---

## Wellness Ranch: Cross-Tabulation Research Question

For the Wellness Ranch CEP project, our team has access to Google Analytics 4.

GA4 tracks website traffic and engagement patterns that can be used to examine visitors' interactions with the website.

A useful research question is:

**Is device category associated with whether a website session is engaged?**

The variables are:

- **Device category:** Desktop, mobile, tablet, or other categories recorded by GA4.
- **Engagement status:** Engaged or not engaged.

The analysis will examine whether engagement patterns differ across device categories.

---

## Research Hypotheses

The hypotheses are:

**Null hypothesis (H0):**

Device category and engagement status are independent.

**Alternative hypothesis (H1):**

Device category and engagement status are associated.

The analysis uses a chi-square test of independence when appropriate.

A statistically significant result would provide evidence of an association between the two variables, but would not establish that device category causes differences in engagement.

---

## Understanding GA4 Engagement

In GA4, an engaged session generally meets at least one of the following conditions:

::: {.incremental}
- The session lasts longer than 10 seconds.
- The session contains a key event.
- The session includes at least two page or screen views.
:::

These criteria make engaged sessions a useful indicator of website interaction.

For Wellness Ranch, examining engagement by device could help identify whether visitors using different devices interact with the website differently.

This information may be relevant when evaluating the mobile and desktop experiences.

---

## Preparing Wellness Ranch GA4 Data

The analysis uses a GA4 export containing session counts by device category and acquisition channel.

```{r}
#| label: ga4-data-status

if (analysis_ready) {

  cat("Wellness Ranch GA4 dataset loaded.\n\n")

  data.frame(
    Measure = c(
      "Export rows",
      "Total sessions",
      "Engaged sessions",
      "Device categories",
      "Acquisition channels"
    ),
    Value = c(
      nrow(ga4),
      sum(ga4$sessions),
      sum(ga4$engaged),
      n_distinct(ga4$device),
      n_distinct(ga4$channel)
    )
  ) |>
    knitr::kable()

} else {

  cat(
    "Our CEP team has GA4 access for Wellness Ranch.\n\n",
    "The required GA4 session-metric export",
    " is not included in this report.\n",
    "Statistical results cannot be established",
    " until the data are imported."
  )
}
```

---

## Cross-Tabulation of Engagement by Device

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wellness-cross
#| tbl-cap: "Website Engagement by Device Category"

if (analysis_ready) {

  device_counts <- ga4 |>
    group_by(device) |>
    summarise(
      Engaged = sum(engaged),
      Not_Engaged = sum(not_engaged),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Total = Engaged + Not_Engaged,
      Engagement_Rate = 100 * Engaged / Total
    )

  device_counts |>
    gt() |>
    tab_header(
      title = "Wellness Ranch Website Engagement",
      subtitle = "Session engagement by device category"
    ) |>
    fmt_number(
      columns = c(Engaged, Not_Engaged, Total),
      decimals = 0
    ) |>
    fmt_number(
      columns = Engagement_Rate,
      decimals = 1
    )

} else {

  cat(
    "Cross-tabulation requires the Wellness Ranch",
    " GA4 session export."
  )
}
```

---

## Visualizing Engagement Across Devices

```{r}
#| label: fig-wellness-engagement
#| fig-cap: "Engagement Rate Across Device Categories"
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5

if (analysis_ready) {

  ggplot(
    device_counts,
    aes(
      x = reorder(device, Engagement_Rate),
      y = Engagement_Rate
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(
      fill = teal,
      width = 0.7
    ) +
    geom_text(
      aes(
        label = paste0(
          round(Engagement_Rate, 1),
          "%"
        )
      ),
      hjust = -0.15,
      size = 5
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(0, 110)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "Wellness Ranch Website Engagement",
      subtitle = "Percentage of engaged sessions by device",
      x = "Device Category",
      y = "Engagement Rate (%)"
    )

} else {

  cat(
    "The engagement chart will be generated",
    " from the GA4 export once available."
  )
}
```

---

## Chi-Square Test of Association

```{r}
#| label: chi-square-test

if (analysis_ready) {

  observed <- as.matrix(
    device_counts[, c("Engaged", "Not_Engaged")]
  )

  rownames(observed) <- as.character(
    device_counts$device
  )

  valid_table <- nrow(observed) >= 2 &&
    all(colSums(observed) > 0) &&
    all(rowSums(observed) > 0)

  if (valid_table) {

    initial_test <- suppressWarnings(
      chisq.test(observed, correct = FALSE)
    )

    if (any(initial_test$expected < 5)) {

      association_test <- chisq.test(
        observed,
        simulate.p.value = TRUE,
        B = 10000
      )

    } else {

      association_test <- initial_test

    }

    cat(
      "Test:", association_test$method, "\n"
    )

    cat(
      "Chi-square statistic:",
      round(
        unname(association_test$statistic),
        3
      ),
      "\n"
    )

    cat(
      "p-value:",
      signif(association_test$p.value, 4),
      "\n\n"
    )

    if (association_test$p.value < 0.05) {

      cat(
        "The results provide evidence",
        " of an association between",
        " device category and engagement status."
      )

    } else {

      cat(
        "The results do not provide",
        " sufficient evidence of an association",
        " between device category and",
        " engagement status."
      )

    }

  } else {

    cat(
      "The available export does not contain",
      " enough categories for this test."
    )
  }

} else {

  cat(
    "A chi-square test has been specified,",
    " but cannot be calculated without",
    " observed GA4 session counts."
  )
}
```

---

## Interpretation of the Cross-Tabulation

The objective of this analysis is to determine whether engagement status differs across device categories for Wellness Ranch website sessions.

The most important descriptive measures are the number of engaged and non-engaged sessions and the engagement rate within each device category.

A chi-square test can then evaluate whether the distribution of engagement status is statistically associated with device category.

Since the actual GA4 export has not been provided for this reflection, I cannot report an observed chi-square statistic or claim a significant relationship.

However, the analysis establishes a reproducible framework that can be applied to the client's data.

---

## Business Implications for Wellness Ranch

If website engagement differs meaningfully across devices, the findings could help Wellness Ranch identify opportunities to improve the visitor experience.

Potential business applications include:

::: {.incremental}
- Examining whether mobile visitors engage differently from desktop visitors.
- Reviewing mobile navigation and page usability.
- Investigating differences in acquisition-channel performance.
- Prioritizing website improvements using engagement evidence.
:::

A significant statistical association alone would not identify the cause of any differences. Additional website performance and user-experience analysis would still be needed.

::: notes
Explain how engagement data can guide investigation without assuming that statistical association proves causation.
:::

---

# Prompt 4: Multiple Regression Analysis

## Essay Prompt 4

> Using the MSDM CEP data, run multiple regression. The dependent variable can be continuous or dichotomous. Regress a dependent variable on a set of independent variables. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.

---

## Wellness Ranch: Multiple Regression Research Question

For the regression analysis, I would examine factors associated with average session duration on the Wellness Ranch website.

**Research question:**

How are website traffic volume, device category, and acquisition channel associated with average session duration?

The analysis uses the following variables:

| Role | Variable |
|---|---|
| Dependent | Average session duration |
| Independent 1 | Number of sessions |
| Independent 2 | Device category |
| Independent 3 | Session default channel group |

This analysis uses multiple linear regression because the dependent variable is continuous.

---

## Regression Model

The model can be expressed as:

\[
\text{Duration}_i =
\beta_0 +
\beta_1\log(1+\text{Sessions}_i) +
\boldsymbol{\beta}_2\text{Device}_i +
\boldsymbol{\beta}_3\text{Channel}_i +
\varepsilon_i
\]

The model examines how average session duration varies with traffic volume, device category, and acquisition channel.

Categorical predictors are represented using indicator variables.

Using the logarithm of session counts can help reduce the influence of extremely large traffic-volume differences.

This model estimates associations, not causal effects.

---

## Why Multiple Regression Is Useful

Multiple regression is useful because website behavior may be related to several factors simultaneously.

For example, website engagement may vary by both device and acquisition channel.

Analyzing these factors together allows the model to estimate relationships while accounting for the other included predictors.

For Wellness Ranch, this approach could provide a more complete picture than examining individual metrics separately.

However, model interpretation must account for the level of aggregation in GA4 exports and the quality of the available data.

---

## Running the Regression Model

```{r}
#| label: wellness-regression-model

if (regression_ready) {

  regression_data <- ga4 |>
    filter(
      is.finite(duration),
      is.finite(sessions),
      sessions > 0
    ) |>
    mutate(
      log_sessions = log1p(sessions)
    )

  regression_model <- lm(
    duration ~ log_sessions + device + channel,
    data = regression_data,
    weights = sessions
  )

  regression_summary <- summary(regression_model)

  print(regression_summary)

} else {

  cat(
    "The regression model is specified",
    " for Wellness Ranch GA4 data.\n\n",
    "It requires sufficient observations",
    " across device and acquisition-channel",
    " categories to estimate the model."
  )
}
```

---

## Regression Results Using gtsummary

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wellness-regression
#| tbl-cap: "Regression Model for Wellness Ranch Session Duration"

if (regression_ready) {

  regression_model |>
    tbl_regression(
      intercept = TRUE,
      estimate_fun = label_style_number(
        digits = 3
      )
    ) |>
    bold_labels()

} else {

  cat(
    "Regression coefficients, confidence",
    " intervals, and p-values will be",
    " calculated from the GA4 export."
  )
}
```

---

## Regression Coefficient Visualization

```{r}
#| label: fig-wellness-regression
#| fig-cap: "Regression Coefficients with Confidence Intervals"
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5

if (regression_ready) {

  coefficients <- broom::tidy(
    regression_model,
    conf.int = TRUE
  ) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    filter(
      !is.na(estimate),
      is.finite(conf.low),
      is.finite(conf.high)
    )

  ggplot(
    coefficients,
    aes(
      x = reorder(term, estimate),
      y = estimate
    )
  ) +
    geom_pointrange(
      aes(
        ymin = conf.low,
        ymax = conf.high
      ),
      color = teal,
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = 0,
      linetype = "dashed",
      color = navy
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      title = "Factors Associated with Session Duration",
      subtitle = "Coefficient estimates and 95% confidence intervals",
      x = "Predictor",
      y = "Estimated Coefficient"
    )

} else {

  cat(
    "Coefficient visualization requires",
    " the Wellness Ranch GA4 regression data."
  )
}
```

---

## Regression Model Fit

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regression-fit
#| tbl-cap: "Wellness Ranch Regression Model Fit"

if (regression_ready) {

  model_fit <- broom::glance(
    regression_model
  )

  data.frame(
    Statistic = c(
      "R-squared",
      "Adjusted R-squared",
      "F-statistic",
      "Model p-value",
      "Observations"
    ),
    Value = c(
      round(model_fit$r.squared, 3),
      round(model_fit$adj.r.squared, 3),
      round(model_fit$statistic, 3),
      signif(model_fit$p.value, 3),
      model_fit$nobs
    )
  ) |>
    knitr::kable()

} else {

  cat(
    "Model performance statistics",
    " cannot be reported until the",
    " regression has been estimated."
  )
}
```

---

## Interpretation of Multiple Regression

The purpose of this analysis is to understand how multiple website characteristics relate to average session duration.

The regression coefficients estimate associations between each predictor and average session duration while controlling for the other included predictors.

A positive coefficient indicates a higher predicted duration, while a negative coefficient indicates a lower predicted duration, subject to the predictor's coding.

Statistical significance and confidence intervals help assess the uncertainty associated with the estimates.

Because the GA4 export is not yet available in this report, I cannot identify statistically significant predictors or quantify the model's explanatory power.

The analysis is therefore specified but does not yet provide empirical regression findings.

---

## Important Statistical Considerations

GA4 exports frequently contain aggregated data instead of individual visitor observations.

This creates several considerations:

::: {.incremental}
- Aggregated observations may not be statistically independent.
- Device and channel groups may differ substantially in size.
- Weighted regression may be useful when rows represent different numbers of sessions.
- Regression assumptions and residual patterns should be evaluated.
- Associations should not be interpreted as proof of causation.
:::

For this reason, the proposed model is best treated as an exploratory analysis until the data structure and assumptions have been examined.

---

## Business Implications of Regression

If an appropriate regression model identifies meaningful relationships, Wellness Ranch may be able to use the results to guide additional marketing investigation.

Potential applications include:

- Comparing visitor behavior across acquisition channels.
- Evaluating differences between desktop and mobile sessions.
- Identifying traffic segments associated with longer visits.
- Investigating opportunities to improve visitor engagement.

The goal is not to maximize a single metric without context.

Instead, the analysis should help Wellness Ranch better understand how visitors interact with its website and which questions deserve further attention.

# Overall Reflection

## What I Learned from Module 08

Module 08 reinforced three important lessons.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

**First, statistical reporting is part of data analysis.**

Results become more valuable when they are organized clearly and presented consistently.

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

**Second, different statistical methods answer different questions.**

Cross-tabulation is useful for categorical associations, while multiple regression can examine relationships involving several predictors.

:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}

**Third, results must be interpreted in context.**

Statistical significance alone does not explain what a finding means for an organization.

:::

---

The Wellness Ranch project provides a practical opportunity to apply these concepts.

Our access to GA4 makes it possible to examine visitor engagement and digital marketing performance using real client data.

This module helped me recognize how statistical tables and models could improve the quality of our reporting.

Rather than simply reporting traffic or engagement metrics, we can formulate research questions and evaluate whether patterns are supported by the data.

The techniques from Module 08 could therefore help our team produce more organized, transparent, and useful client-facing analysis.
